Chapter 8: Reinventing the Company—Digital Transformation and the Internet Age
The late 1990s brought on a whole new kind of challenge for the company—one that would ask everyone to rethink what they knew and how they worked. Suddenly, the internet and digital technology were changing entire industries almost overnight. And just like that, the old ways of doing business? They were quickly fading into the past.
Inside the company, you could feel this mix of excitement and a bit of unease. Some folks saw the digital revolution as a real threat, maybe even something to fear. But others? They looked at it as the biggest opportunity they’d seen in a generation. The leader understood that standing still just wasn’t an option. He put it simply: If we don’t disrupt ourselves, someone else will.
So, the push for digital transformation started small. Teams began tinkering with new software, dipping their toes into e-commerce, and really thinking about new ways to connect with their customers. Picture a group of engineers late at night, gathered around a glowing screen, debating how to bring an old, familiar product into the digital era. Those first attempts? They were clunky, sure. But every failure got them a little bit closer to that breakthrough moment.
What became obvious pretty quickly was that digital transformation isn’t just about the tools or the tech. It’s really about a new way of thinking. The company needed to become more agile, more open to taking risks, and more willing to try new ideas. The old hierarchies started to break down, replaced by cross-functional teams. And with that, the pace of change started to pick up—fast.
There was this one moment that really stood out. A long-serving manager, who’d always been a bit skeptical about the internet, stood up in a meeting. He shared how his team had used new digital tools to finally solve a problem that had blocked them for years. The whole room burst into applause—not just because they’d found a solution, but because he’d shown what it meant to embrace change.
You know, most people really underestimate just how hard it is to let go of the familiar. But the company’s journey through the digital age proved something powerful: reinvention can happen at any stage, no matter how established you are.
So here’s the key takeaway—the future belongs to those who are willing to learn, adapt, and keep moving forward.
